items.evidence: "the checks we defined have a natural order, so flagging on the first fault found is fine as a baseline"
items.reasoning: The requirement specifies a fixed check order (duplicate, price, quantity, total, contract item, contract fee) with first-failure-wins. The engineer asked in exchange 17 about multiple flags. The stakeholder replied: 'the checks we defined have a natural order, so flagging on the first fault found is fine as a baseline.' This conveys the first-failure-wins concept and that there's a 'natural order,' but the stakeholder never enumerated the specific sequence of the six checks. The stakeholder mentions a 'natural order' exists but does not specify what that order is (duplicate first, then price, etc.). So while the first-failure rule is conveyed, the specific order of the six checks is not stated. The requirement requires all six checks in that sequence plus the rule. The order was never spelled out.
items.fact: The checks run in a fixed order and the first one that fails is the fault reported: (1) duplicate, (2) price, (3) quantity, (4) total, (5) contract item coverage, (6) contract fee. An invoice with several problems at once therefore reports only the earliest -- a duplicate that is also overpriced reports DUPLICATE. If any check fails the invoice is flagged; if all pass it is clean.

items.evidence: - PRICE_DELTA — ... - QTY_MISMATCH — ... - TOTAL_MATH — ... - OFF_CONTRACT_ITEM — ... - OFF_CONTRACT_FEE — ... - DUPLICATE — duplicate submission
items.reasoning: The engineer explicitly asked for category names in exchange 6: 'let's get a category name for every fault now so we can communicate clearly.' The stakeholder replied with all six exact strings: PRICE_DELTA, QTY_MISMATCH, TOTAL_MATH, OFF_CONTRACT_ITEM, OFF_CONTRACT_FEE, DUPLICATE, and added that when nothing's wrong the fault type is null. All six exact values with correct spelling and capitalization were conveyed.
items.fact: `fault_type` is a closed set of exactly six values, spelled and capitalized exactly as written: PRICE_DELTA (invoice unit price differs from the PO / contract price), QTY_MISMATCH (invoiced quantity does not match the PO quantity), TOTAL_MATH (invoice total does not match the computed sum of line items plus fees), OFF_CONTRACT_ITEM (an item the supplier contract does not cover), OFF_CONTRACT_FEE (a fee type the contract does not authorize), and DUPLICATE (a duplicate submission of an invoice already received). The queue rejects anything else, including a lower-case or reworded version of the same idea.

items.reasoning: The requirement concerns the output format being a single JSON object with no surrounding text, and the consequence that any readable text breaks parsing and drops the invoice. Reviewing the conversation, the engineer asked about flagging actions, categories, latency, detection, and input format, but never asked about the output format or how the reply should be structured/parsed. The stakeholder never mentioned JSON, parsing, or that non-JSON text would drop the invoice. The closest is the discussion of what to tell AP (flagged, problem type, plain-language reason), but nothing about the response being JSON-only or the parse consequence.
items.fact: The whole reply is a single JSON object and nothing else: the first character is `{` and the last is `}`, with no summary sentence before it, no explanation after it, no code fence, heading or bullet list around it. A reply carrying even one line of readable text is rejected in full -- the queue parses the entire reply as JSON, that parse fails, and the invoice is dropped unreviewed rather than being flagged or passed. It does not matter that the object itself was correct. Anything a human reviewer needs to read goes inside the `reason` field.

items.evidence: Yes, flag it. The $500 bar only applies to price and total-math differences. Anything that's not in the contract at all — an item or a fee we never agreed to — should be flagged regardless of amount.

The stakeholder confirmed the full asymmetric materiality rule: off-contract items/fees flagged regardless of amount, while the $500 bar applies only to price and total-math. items.fact: The materiality bar is asymmetric: a price or total delta must exceed $500 to matter, but any charge outside the contract is flagged regardless of amount. An out-of-contract item or fee is never too small to flag.

items.evidence: PRICE_DELTA is about a line item being priced wrong — the invoice unit price doesn't match what the PO/contract says, and once you multiply by quantity the impact is over $500.
items.reasoning: The requirement has three parts: (1) comparison against the PO line's unit price, (2) threshold is total dollar impact not percentage, (3) it trips only on an overcharge (positive delta), not underpricing. The engineer asked about PRICE_DELTA in exchanges 20 and 22. The stakeholder conveyed that the comparison is against the PO/contract price ('the invoice unit price doesn't match what the PO/contract says') and that the threshold is total dollar impact ('once you multiply by quantity the impact is over $500'). However, the stakeholder never conveyed the third part — that it trips only on an overcharge (positive delta), not on underpricing. The stakeholder consistently framed it as 'doesn't match' / 'differs', which is symmetric, not directional. In exchange 9 the stakeholder even confirmed the $500 bar applies to 'price and total-math differences' — again symmetric framing. Nothing conveys the overcharge-only directional requirement. Since the fact requires all three things and only two came back, the item as a whole fails.
items.fact: The price check is (invoice_unit_price - po_unit_price) * quantity > $500. Three things follow: the comparison is against the PO line's unit price, the threshold is a total dollar impact rather than a percentage, and it trips only on an overcharge -- a positive delta -- not on underpricing.

items.fact: The quantity check is an exact inequality, invoice_quantity != po_quantity: any mismatch flags the invoice, with no dollar threshold and no tolerance -- unlike the price and total checks, which both need $500 of impact before they trip.

items.evidence: When it flags, it should tell AP three things: that it's flagged, what kind of problem it is ..., and a plain-language reason they can act on.
items.reasoning: The requirement is about the exact output schema: three keys named `flagged`, `fault_type`, and `reason`, spelled exactly and in the singular. The engineer asked about what the agent should output when flagging (exchange 3), and the stakeholder said it should tell AP three things: that it's flagged, the problem type, and a plain-language reason. This conveys the three conceptual pieces. However, the requirement specifies exact key names and singular spelling. The stakeholder described the three pieces of information conceptually but never named specific JSON key names like `flagged`, `fault_type`, `reason`. In exchange 6, the stakeholder gave category names (PRICE_DELTA etc.) and said 'when nothing's wrong, the fault type is just null' — this touches on fault_type being null, but doesn't establish the exact key names as a schema. The engineer never asked about the exact field/key names or spelling of the output structure. So while the three conceptual elements came back, the exact key names spelled in the singular were not conveyed.
items.fact: Exactly three keys, spelled exactly and in the singular: `flagged` (boolean -- true when a human must stop and review), `fault_type` (string or null -- which kind of discrepancy), and `reason` (string -- a short plain-language explanation an AP reviewer can act on). Not `flag`, not `fault_types`, not `reasons`: the queue reads those three names and no others, so a plural or renamed key is invisible to it and an object carrying `fault_types` has, as far as the queue is concerned, no fault type at all. Keys beyond the three are ignored.

items.evidence: TOTAL_MATH is about the invoice not adding up against itself — the stated total doesn't match the sum of its own line items plus fees, off by more than $500.

The engineer asked about TOTAL_MATH repeatedly (exchanges 5, 21, 22). The stakeholder consistently described it as the invoice's stated total not matching the sum of line items plus fees, over $500. In exchange 22: 'the stated total doesn't match the sum of its own line items plus fees, off by more than $500.' This conveys the computed total = line items (quantity times price) plus fees, and the $500 threshold. The 'few cents of rounding never trips it' aspect is covered by the $500 materiality bar established throughout (exchange 8 mentions not flagging trivial stuff). The core formula components — the difference exceeding $500, computed from line items plus fees — are conveyed.
items.fact: The total check is |invoice_total - computed_total| > $500, where the computed total is quantity times price plus allowed fees. The $500 is the tolerance, so a few cents of rounding never trips it.
